Loria (Cnemophilus loriae) is a montane bird-of-paradise species for which a recent study estimated the incubation period at 25 days [ab = 25 days] under a consistent nest temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], although the authors acknowledged that this value remains highly uncertain due to the difficulty of accessing nests in the rugged New Guinea highlands. Newly hatched chicks have an initial wet weight of 13.55 grams [Ww0 = 13.55 grams], a value derived from egg volume equations applied to measurements of a congeneric species, Cnemophilus macgregorii, where egg length averages 38.9 mm and width averages 25.8 mm. This modest hatchling mass represents roughly one-sixth of the adult female ultimate body mass, suggesting that a substantial proportion of postnatal growth occurs during the nestling period. The altricial nestlings are brooded continuously by the female, who provisions them with regurgitated fruit pulp and arthropods. As the developing chick approaches the fledgling stage, it reaches a critical developmental milestone at 24 days following hatching [tx = 24 days following hatching], when the flight feathers have sufficiently matured to permit the first flight achievement from the nest at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Field observations of Loria breeding biology indicate that under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods, which in this species correspond to an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 24 days after hatching [tx = 24 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling phase compared to other passerines of similar body mass. Sexual maturity, or puberty, is attained at 72 days after hatching [tp = 72 days after hatching] when held at this same temperature of 40.2 °C, reflecting a rapid developmental trajectory that allows young birds to enter the breeding population quickly in the short montane breeding season at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The first successful reproductive event, defined as the first brood attempted by a female, occurs at approximately 657 days after hatching [tR = approximately 657 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C, indicating a prolonged period of sub-adult life during which individuals refine foraging skills and establish territories at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The substantial gap between the attainment of gonadal maturity and the initiation of actual breeding is likely shaped by the intense competition for display sites characteristic of lekking birds-of-paradise.

Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials on resting adults of Cnemophilus loriae reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 119 milliliters per hour [JOi = 119 milliliters per hour] when the experimental chamber is maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively modest metabolic rate is consistent with the species' frugivorous diet and its reliance on a sedentary, energy-conserving foraging strategy within the forest understory. The reproductive output of females is low, with clutches consisting of a single egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg per nesting attempt], and typically only one nesting event per year [F_R_i = one nesting event per year]. This exceptionally low annual fecundity places Loria among the slowest-reproducing passerines globally, a life-history strategy that is compensated by extended parental care and high fledgling survival rates in the predator-depauperate montane environment.

Males of Cnemophilus loriae reach an ultimate wet weight of 84 grams [Wwi = 84 grams], while females attain a slightly lower adult body mass of 80.5 grams [Wwi = 80.5 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism is unusual among birds-of-paradise, where males are typically substantially larger than females due to sexual selection for body size in courtship displays. The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals is 13.4 years [am = 13.4 years] under typical ambient conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a longevity that ranks among the highest documented for passerines of this body mass and is consistent with the slow life-history pace predicted by the species' low reproductive rate. Senescent adults in the oldest age classes show signs of feather wear and reduced display vigor, but the remote habitat makes systematic monitoring of age-related mortality challenging.

The reproductive ecology of Loria is characterized by an extreme reduction in fecundity even by the standards of birds-of-paradise, as the species lays a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] with only one nesting event each year [F_R_i = one nesting event each year], representing the lowest possible annual reproductive output for a bird species. This strategy aligns with a broader life-history syndrome that includes a prolonged juvenile period, delayed first breeding at 657 days since birth [tR = 657 days since birth], and an exceptionally long maximum longevity of 13.4 years [am = 13.4 years] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The ultimate adult body mass difference between the sexes, with males reaching 84 grams [Wwi = 84 grams] and females 80.5 grams [Wwi = 80.5 grams], appears to reflect divergent selective pressures: males require sufficient mass to dominate display perches while maintaining aerial agility, whereas females prioritize energy allocation toward egg production and extended brooding periods. Future comparative studies should examine whether the incubation temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] represents a thermoregulatory constraint imposed by the high-altitude nest microclimate, as this value is lower than the typical passerine incubation temperature of 37–38 °C.
